But where there has been a suggestion of inconsistency, a Court would then be entitled to look at those statements and say whether, in actual fact, the witness himself has been inconsistent, as suggested. It then really begs the question: How does that affect the witness's evidence in toto. So while I submit, and perhaps an easy option is to say: It merely goes to credibility, and clearly it does go to credibility, in my submission there is scope for the Court to attribute to his evidence vis-a-vis the context of the other statements the weight and value of the account that he gives. And I would seek to rely upon the Rules in relation to that. May I just obtain that rule? If one looks at Rule 89(F), and I read for everyone's assistance. "A Chamber may receive the evidence of a witness orally or, where the interests of justice lie, in written form." Well, clearly there has been evidence which my learned friend relies upon to demonstrate his inconsistency, and therefore I would submit when one looks at the totality of the problem that now goes before the Court, if it be a problem, then, in our submission, it would be an appropriate course. And it does not have to be merely for consistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, 89(F) would normally not be regarded as relevant to the question of tendering of a document that had been the subject of cross-examination. The normal practice of the Tribunal where a document is put in cross-examination for the purpose of identifying what appears to be a change of substance of account is to have the material passage read into the transcript and then to have the witness comment on the change and not to tender the document itself. In this case, I would suggest to you the material distinction from -- that might justify a different course is the express proposition not only that there has been some change of account, but that on more than one material issue there has been recent invention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will be actually making a submission in relation to that latter category in relation to another matter to rebut the presumption of invention. I understand that that is one of the exceptions to the common-law rule. And I, for my part, am quite happy for it to go in on that basis. It is a very unusual set of circumstances that we find ourselves in; I cannot think of a specific authority that deals with it. But certainly to rebut the presumption of fabrication is one of the categories that would allow it in, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think, if you analyse it, Mr. Moore, that goes down to credibility in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour's, I'm sure, a much better lawyer than I will ever be, and that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Flattery won't get you very far, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It never has, I fear, but there we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any comment about the previous statement and the transcript of the evidence of the witness should be received as an exhibit? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must express some reservations. I am speaking on my own behalf. I have not had time to confer with my colleagues. I complied with the rules that you set down, Your Honour, that inconsistent portions of any statement that a witness can be confronted with. In the interest of the Defence and in relation to this witness, I would agree to have his entire statement submitted. But if we leave this as an exception, this will be a precedent for all further situations. And this is something the Chamber must be aware of, too. I suspect the further and further we go there will be more and more witnesses with varying accounts and testimonies, and I'm referring to the Prosecution witness and the possible Defence witnesses. The substance of this trial has already been discussed in virtually three different trials, and the credibility of the witnesses is an issue that is likely to be raised again and again throughout the trial. The OTP leads the witness on examination-in-chief. When it's my witness, I take the witness through it in order to prove my case. I have some portions that I wish to show the Trial Chamber. I have inconsistencies to point out. I have discrepancies to draw the Chamber's attention to. If we make an exception here, and I am aware of the extent of documents and materials from all the different trials, I'm sure that there will always be someone having doubts about a witness's credibility. I believe we should stick to what we started out doing, for portions of statements to be put and for this to be available to both parties. I believe we should stick to that principle otherwise we are likely to be facing a huge amount of problems because there will be so many different accounts by different persons and different accounts by the same persons about the relevant events. That is what I am afraid of, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I well understand your concern. That is why the practice that has become, as I understand it, pretty uniform in this Tribunal is not to receive previous full statements but merely to identify those parts that are material. It not only confines then the potential more debate and discussion within the trial, but it also makes it easier should there be an appeal, for the Appeals Chamber to see what was the point in the issue. There are two limbs to that reasoning. Is there any other submission? Mr. Moore, before ruling on the matter, you will realise that the Chamber has not seen any of these documents and your comment earlier is one that appeals to us as potentially the way forward, that is to have offered to us a marked-up version, one that, by consultation between yourself and Defence counsel, has identified those passages which appear material to these disputed issues, and that is the issues where there has been a change of story or there is a proposition of recent invention. We can then see quickly whether the context is going to assist us to evaluate particularly the recent invention proposition. If it is not, we will maintain the normal position; but if it is going to be material and assist us, the circumstances might well justify receiving the document. So we will not make a decision on the matter at this point; we will wait until the -- an agreed marked-up version of each of the documents can be made available, and we will see then whether it should be received. But if it is received, Mr. Moore, it will be to the issue of credit only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept the Court's ruling. I have no problems, obviously, in relation to that, although it might be interesting for the Court to remember that in England now under the new criminal justice act 2003 that there is a variation in relation to the hearsay rules and what is hearsay and what is not, what can be relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but we are running here on our Rules, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I am really very grateful. I never understood very much. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, you have told us that you have said at Belgrade, at the court there, that in relation to Kijanovic, Tomic, and, in particular, Borisavljevic, that you had said to Borisavljevic to go and get Mrksic; but you have told this Court clearly that that was not the case, he was not there. And you have given an account of why you have said that. Can I deal with that issue for one moment then, please. How difficult was it for you to give evidence in Belgrade about this matter and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My learned friend, in putting this question to the witness, told the witness that he sent Borisavljevic to go get Mrksic. He didn't say that, nor is this recorded in any of the statements. He wasn't supposed to go get Mrksic, just go inform Mrksic that a unit of military police is needed. This is what I wanted to object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I accept that. I hope the substance remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you found it difficult to give evidence in Belgrade about these topics?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I will give you just one sentence. The first time when I was summoned to testify about the Ovcara case in front of the president of the war trial, then-colonel, and later General Gojevic, my position was that I shouldn't testify -- in fact, I refused to testify. I told him they should designate a cell for me, that I wanted to be the accused, and I wanted my role to be proven as well as my activities and how I went about implementing my assignment. This was three days after the state of war was declared, after the NATO bombing had started. Then, with the president of the war court, I managed to convince him to give up on interviewing me as a witness because it was extremely difficult for me to testify. I knew exactly -- or rather, I anticipated exactly what kind of pressure I would be put under because I was asked to testify only three days after the war against Yugoslavia had erupted. I was asked to testify about the events in Vukovar and Ovcara. I don't know how many other persons were summoned to testify about these events at the time. Based on what I heard, only Major Lukic was called, as well as another journalist to testified perhaps not in front of many Chamber. I apologise. I refused to testify on that occasion, and I waited for the next summons, which came after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question - and thank you for that, it's part of the answer. But can I just ask you to focus on the question. Here you are. You've had Mr. Lukic ask you questions, perfectly reasonably, saying: Here you are in Belgrade. You say that you spoke to Borisavljevic. But of course here, in giving your evidence, you said when you called for him he wasn't there. Now, there's a difference, and of course the Prosecution accept that. But what I want you to answer is that when you were actually giving evidence on this topic, how difficult was it for you, as a Serb, to give evidence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extremely difficult. It was extremely difficult, truly. It was so difficult that you can see what I stated in that trial. I believe that the president of the chamber understood just how difficult it was to me. He guided me and encouraged me to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you then, please, you also said that you were going to tell this Trial Chamber on who tried to put pressure on you not to tell the truth. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all Defence counsel had my statements at their disposal, both those given before the military court and those given to the Prosecution. I said that on behalf of the military portion, the commission for -- or rather, the national commission for cooperation, a representative of that commission was present there throughout the whole time. He took me to the interview with the OTP. His name was Colonel Mojsilovic. He was present there throughout the whole time. Perhaps he went out briefly, but he received the statement I gave to The Hague Prosecution. Colonel Mojsilovic had the same statement that can be found here. My statement was assessed from that point of view. I was also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- called by the commission. I was invited to come to an interview with the commission, to talk to them about the statement. I can also say this, and I hope that Mr. Vasic will not misinterpret this. When Lieutenant-Colonel Panic called me to, as he put it, reconcile our statements, that was another difficult situation for me. I warned both of them and said that my first statement given to the president of the military court was sent with the whole file to the OTP. So I didn't send this statement on my own, no. It was sent officially with the whole file, as part of a file against unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, you have been cross-examined by Mr. Lukic about a statement that you say Mr. Sljivancanin made as you were leaving the -- what I will call the first meeting at Negoslavci. That was the statement that dealt with Sljivancanin saying: Don't be surprised if you see Chetniks slaughtering people. I use that in general terms. Now, do you follow? You've told this Court about that particular statement. It's not in your witness statement at OTP, it is not mentioned in any of your court transcripts. Why -- if, as you say, that you wanted -- or you've had it for 14 years, why didn't you tell the OTP investigators or the judge about what Sljivancanin had said when he was leaving or when you were leaving Negoslavci about slaughtering by the Chetniks? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. This, again, is a very important question about how I presented facts. To this day I'm not sure whether Vojvoda Topola is still alive. None of the councillors or Mr. Sljivancanin ever informed me about who Vojvoda Topola actually is. Perhaps I'm yet to meet him or perhaps he will surprise me by doing something. Is he going to benevolently interpret my words and description of events. I don't know that. But this is a reason why I never mentioned this before the military court or the special court. I opted to say here what I experienced and heard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any fear that anything would happen to you if, in actual fact, you had publicly stated what Sljivancanin said about the Chetniks slaughtering?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, of course. Everybody knows how tightly Major Sljivancanin was defended before his arrest or during his arrest in Belgrade. One of my neighbours told me about this. He was present or he was in a group protecting Major Sljivancanin. He belongs to this association called Sloboda. He is a big man, 2 metres, and is a chef in a major Belgrade hotel. So I had to wonder whether he approached me accidentally to discuss such issues with me such as who is a traitor, who is a patriot, what is the right thing to do, and so on. These were daily occurrences. One could experience this on a daily basis in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I just deal then, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, this perhaps more for the Court at this stage because I want to deal with Colonel Mrksic. In my submission, the Defence have not put to this witness whether they accept, as this witness has said, that the Velepromet facility was within, what I will call, the zone of responsibility for Mrksic. This witness says that that is the case. In our submission, if that is not the case, that that should be put by Mrksic's counsel to this witness so he has an opportunity to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the course of cross-examination to be as you indicate, Mr. Moore. Perhaps I could confirm that with Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can I just say that I would apply the same principle: Do they accept that the JNA barracks are within the zone of responsibility for Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As for the question put by my learned friend, I can say that the Defence of General Mrksic does not dispute that General Mrksic was commander of the Operations Group South, within whose area of responsibility Velepromet and barracks were. But the Defence clearly disputed through its questions as well as through the arrangement that we made where we split topics between the Defence counsel, and within that we disputed that the JNA was stationed throughout the whole time at Velepromet and that there was a staff of the Vukovar TO Defence there. As for the operations area, both Kasrna [as interpreted] and Velepromet were located within the area of operations of the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, barracks and Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is, I understand it, that the barracks and Velepromet, both of them were located within the area of operations of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, the zone of responsibility for Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, could I just ask you then - and moving on in topic - how important is it for a commander to know what is occurring in his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All military rules are directed towards ensuring that. All organs subordinated to the commander are duty-bound to inform him whenever there is a change in the situation or to inform him about a new situation. This is all well known. These rules are there to ensure that legal procedure is complied with, to ensure effectiveness of command. Commander must be in a charge of a situation, must be informed of all changes. He also must be warned about what is anticipated. Therefore, the work of all organs is directed towards that goal. Even his superior command issues guidance along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Okay. So how -- you've dealt with it slightly, but how is -- how is that achieved within a military structure? How is the command and control achieved within the zone of responsibility when one deals with the control and command of the commander himself?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the commander assesses a situation and decides on his own. The decision that he takes he needs to take to the superior in order for it to be approved. If the commander and the command are at a high level, and if it has to do with an important stage of the operations, important enough to ensure that the superior command approves this and approves the assignments given to units, then the commander is duty-bound to ensure approval for all this. I believe that Colonel Mrksic, in the final stages of the Vukovar operation, had to harmonise or had to ensure that the decision he took was approved by the superior command and superior commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about the subordination of units to a commander? How does one command and control those units? What are the principles that guide that in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave evidence before this Trial Chamber, saying that in accordance with Article 112 of the law on All People's Defence, the principles of command are clearly set forth. The first principle is the unity of command to ensure that all resources and all forces are aimed at achieving the set goal. In that sense, the commander within his area of responsibility is the most senior officer. He is the one giving assignments to subordinate commanders and units. His decisions must be implemented, his orders as well. So the order of a superior is a law to those who are subordinated to him. The authorities of the commander can be transferred to his deputies only in cases regulated by law or by rules. I explained that Colonel Mrksic transferred his task related to briefing to Major Sljivancanin. That is to say that Major Sljivancanin conveyed the task to us, the task that he received from his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if that is the case, from what you understood in your dealings there, to whom was Sljivancanin subordinated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was subordinated to Colonel Mrksic. As for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to whom was Borisavljevic subordinated --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my impression that the witness wanted to complete his sentence; however, my learned friend interrupted him. Perhaps it would be fair to let him finish his previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript suggests that may be correct, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel what you've said is you've said Sljivancanin was subordinated to Colonel Mrksic. And then you started, by the looks of the transcript, "as for." What were you going to say after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that in the professional sense when it comes to the rules regulating the work of the security organs and their implementation, he is responsible for these tasks to his superior commander in the security chain of command. I don't know who was his first superior in that security chain of command, that is to say professional chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll ask the question again and try and pronounce it again. To whom was Borisavljevic subordinated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borisavljevic was subordinated as a security organ to Major Sljivancanin. This was the professional chain of command. On the other hand, as a subordinate officer he was certainly subordinated to Colonel Mrksic. As for the Velepromet assignment, that specific assignment, I do not know how it was regulated by the order, how the implementation of assignments at Velepromet was regulated. But there had to exist some written order or a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then finally, as far as you could understand from your dealings, to whom was Miodrag Panic subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff within the command of Colonel Mrksic, he was subordinated to Colonel Mrksic. In addition to that, he also had certain authorities as a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'd like to move on to another topic, if I may. I want you to throw your mind back, please, to the evidence that you gave about when you returned to Negoslavci after having witnessed various incidents at Velepromet. Now, Mr. Vasic put the following question to you that you, Colonel, allegedly told Mrksic what you had seen and people being killed. And the answer that you gave was as follows. "I wanted him to hear it." Now, do you remember saying that: "I wanted him to hear it," "him" being Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you want Mrksic to hear the killings at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, had I done it otherwise -- I apologise. Had I done what my fellow officers did, Tomic and Kijanovic, then based on the law, I would be sitting to the left or to the right of Colonel Mrksic answering this question. In accepting the assignment, in accepting to implement the assignment, I invested my full mental and physical faculties in ensuring that the assignment is implemented. I acted the way I did, realising that perhaps I would never come to testify here or thinking that nobody would ever find out what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It may well be it's the way that I phrased the question, but why was it important to tell Colonel Mrksic that what -- that you had seen killing at Velepromet? Why?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to inform him that this happened, which was my duty under the law, to inform the commander that this happened within his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to another question, please, flowing from that. What would you expect him to do or how would you expect him to react, having been told that people were being killed in his zone of responsibility? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. He could have acted based on what I said. He could have failed to act. He could have kept silent, as he did. However, under the law and under the rules of the international law of war, he was duty-bound to take measures to establish the facts. He was duty-bound to find out whether what I told him was true or not. There had to be some verification. Colonel Mrksic had the resources and manpower available to him that were sufficient to establish the truthfulness of this account and to have some form of verification. Under the law, he should have established a committee. He should have appointed officers. He had a legal assistant in his own unit, Colonel Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who had the wartime assignment of infractions and crimes, to establish the identities of those found dead or wounded. I do believe that this was indeed what Lieutenant Jankovic was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is I then please deal with -- it is a 65 ter document, 2 -- number 298. It deals with the 1988 regulations on the applications of international laws of war. I want you to please have a look at these two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist my learned friends I've given the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've got hard copies for you, Colonel. I'm told it's on the splendid e-court, but the hard copies are there as well. The e-court number is 00807698 and 00807699. Now, you can have a hard copy, some people prefer hard copies, or you can look at the wonderful screen. Would you like a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, may I pass this forward then, please. And I hope then having given all the details that the Court will then have the references. No, that's not what -- what I'm expecting to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: While the computer is orientated, would you be kind enough to look at that copy and look at regulation number 20 and regulation 21. It's in front of you. Can you see it all right. Can you answer yes or no, Colonel, have you got it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got the e-court copy, but it's completely -- well, you just can't read it. It's just a fudge. Certainly over here it is. I don't know what the Court -- it's out of focus completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we have the B/C/S on screen. I haven't turned to the English yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure Your Honour will be delighted to read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting for you to proffer the hard copy this way, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't think there are any left. Would Your Honour forgive me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: English is on screen now and it's very clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I've just got it in B/C/S and it's in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's been retrieved from history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll try and do is I'll move over to the side. It looks as if one screen has got some sort of -- that's in B/C/S, and I've got the English. Let's deal with the English, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, would you be kind enough, please, to go to the -- Article Number 20. Have you got it there in front of you? You've got it in hard copy, anyway, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I see this reads: "Prevention of any violations of the international criminal law and criminal responsibility." This is Article 20. "Personal responsibility for any violations of the international laws of war." Do you expect me to read it out loud or do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough -- would you be kind enough to read it out loud. I am going to be asking for it to be made an exhibit, but it does help everybody so that they can hear what you've said. And then I'm going to ask you one or two questions about number 20 and then number 21. Shall we do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article reads: "Any individual, military or civilian, is personally responsible for violations of the rules of the international -- of the laws on war, whoever carries out this violation or issues an order for the violation to occur. Lack of familiarity with the provisions does not preclude criminal responsibility in relation to those violating the provisions." Paragraph 2 reads: "Persons committing a war crime or another serious violation of the rules of war will be prosecuted before their national court or, if they fall into the hands of the enemy, before the enemy's courts." This is an article describing personal responsibility. In continuation, paragraph 3: "The perpetrators of these crimes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have one objection about this. I don't remember this being raised on cross-examination by any of our Defence teams. There was nothing about the norms or the applications of any of the laws or provisions with regard to the subject matter back in 1991. Therefore, I believe my learned friend should have asked questions about this in chief, if he so wanted. But we have so far not even established the existence of these provisions and norms in the constitution of the SFRY at the time. Plus, as I have already pointed out, I don't believe this was raised on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In my submission, it is a natural corollary of the questions that my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, asked. Mr. Vasic asked about: You allegedly told him what you had seen of people being killed. I wanted him to hear it. Well, it is perfectly permissible to ask him why it was he wanted him to hear it, as point one. And point two: Why was that? That is the consequence of that is because it is against the law. And three: In our submission, it is a natural consequence to direct the witness's attention to the actual existing rules for the JNA that were existing at that time having been compiled in 1988. It's a direct consequence of the question of my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, and that's why I quoted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I believe the proposition put by Mr. Moore is soundly based, Mr. Vasic, so we will not interrupt the re-examination. It directly flows, I think you see, from your question, and it is just pinning down the source of this witness's understanding as to the legal requirement. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Colonel, I think we have got to the third paragraph. In English: "The perpetrators of such criminal acts," can you read that, please. Can you carry on reading, would you mind, where you left off?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was listening to the interpret. I'm not sure that I understand properly. You saw some people being killed. I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like you please -- I'd like you please just to stop for a moment, and I want you to continue reading, if you'd be kind enough, this particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The perpetrators of such crimes may be tried before international court, if such a court exists." The next paragraph: "Those persons will also be tried as perpetrators who are found to have instigated, aided, or abetted any violations of the law of war" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "or found to have been involved in the perpetration of such violations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we can put it in completeness, this deals with personal responsibility for violations of war. I think you've already accepted that. Now, let's move on to Article 21, please. Now, I'd like you to read this and then I have a question for you at the end.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 21: "Responsibility for actions taken by subordinates. Any military officer will be personally responsible for violations of the international law of war if he knew or had reason to know that units subordinate to him or other units or other individuals were preparing to commit such violations and for failing to prevent these violations in a timely manner or for failing to take measures in order for these violations to be prevented. Those officers, too, shall be held personally responsible who knew that violations of the international law of war had been committed and failed to -- failed to initiate disciplinary or criminal proceedings against the perpetrators. If no such proceedings are within their purview, then these officers must report the relevant perpetrators to the relevant superior officer." Paragraph 3: "A military commander shall be responsible as an accomplice if, by failing to take measures against his subordinates committing violations of the international rules of law, he contributed to a repeated commission of such acts by his subordinate units or individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I have is this: If we look at Article 21, how important is this article for an officer who discovers that killings are occurring within his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite certain that this article defines the responsibility of a commanding officer for any violations of the international laws of war. And it is quite clear that measures are envisaged that an officer must take against anyone in violation of these rules. The same applies to cases where a commanding officer fails to take steps or initiate proceedings or an investigation against any perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no additional re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you indicate that you proposed to tender those documents, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be tendering those documents. I can put them in now. I am calling an expert called Theunens. He will be adducing these rules in any event, but perhaps just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm quite happy if it's to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I sincerely hope it is. But can I just say that quite simply it will be going in, in a bundle. But if for any reason it is omitted, can I say that I reserve my position of putting these documents in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll wait for the event, Mr. Moore, if there is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I observe that the documents were translated by those here assisting us from B/C/S, I would understand, on the spot, it would seem. As they are legal texts, the precise language is important and the Chamber would be referring to an authorised translation rather than what appears in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- if there is any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes your examination here. The Chamber is grateful that you've been able to attend The Hague and expresses its appreciation of the assistance that you have been able to give to the Chamber. And we thank you, and you are now, of course, free to return to your home. So we will adjourn now, and in a little while you can leave the court after we do. You can be seated for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter; it is entirely my fault. I forgot to put it. I did mention it earlier on. It relates to a document, and there is a submission that I would want to make about it. I suspect that my learned friends may have an argument about it, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a matter that concerns further evidence from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It does, yes. But -- not significantly, but yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must ask you to sit again. There may be one further matter. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to submit but for the witness not to hear what I am going to submit because I would not want it to be thought that my submission in any way may prejudice the Defence. I don't know if that can be done or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It certainly can be. It's a very proper proposition to put. Mr. Vujic, the Prosecutor wants to put some matter to us. He's concerned that he should not speak in your presence in case it could be said to unduly influence you. Would you please go with the court officer, and we will hear what counsel have to say. We will then have a break, and if you're wanted again, you will be advised and will come in after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The submission -- the submission that I would have at this time really relates to the cross-examination of my learned friend on behalf of Mr. Mrksic. What is being put perfectly fairly and perfectly properly is that at no time did Mrksic receive any notice from the Velepromet incident; and then secondly it was put that at no time did Mrksic receive notice from Tomic that incidents were happening at the JNA barracks. May I deal with the second point. Clearly what is being submitted here by the Defence is that this witness is giving a fabricated account, both in relation to the notice after Velepromet, but also in relation to Tomic saying to Mrksic that incidents were happening at the JNA barracks and Mrksic basically played no part or disregarded what was said. And so, putting it quite plainly, what's being said by Mr. Mrksic's counsel is that this witness is not to be believed and what he is saying is a fabricated account. Clearly, therefore, in our submission, the issue of the witness -- witness's credibility is at issue in relation to this matter. We would submit, if that is the case and the issue is one of credibility, that we would be entitled to place before this witness other evidence, namely part of the state [sic] of Tomic, which -- and I can say it now, and that's why I didn't want to do it in front of the witness, which states in actual fact that Tomic went and informed Mrksic of what had happened at the JNA barracks. And the reason we submit it is not because of the truth of its content but because it is entirely consistent with the account given by this witness. And therefore, when you evaluate the overall credibility of this witness, you should disregard it for the truth of the content, but you are entitled to take it into account when consisting -- when considering the consistency of this witness's evidence. So we would submit that there is scope within the Rules for this witness to be reminded of what a person has said and for the Court then to evaluate whether, in actual fact, when one looks at the totality of his credibility, whether in actual fact that is right or not. It is important to note, it was put in the negative by Mr. Vasic. It is not accepted that Tomic told Mrksic about what was happening at the JNA barracks. The Defence are not prejudiced because they have now stated quite categorically that this did not occur, and therefore, that is before the Court. As I say, it only goes to the consistency and the credibility of this witness. Perhaps a better way of putting it is: It goes to the credibility of this witness, and the Court is allowed to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I be clear. What is it you wish to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would wish this witness to read into the record what Tomic has said in relation to Tomic going to Mrksic and informing Mrksic about what had happened at the JNA barracks and the concerns that he has. This witness says that Tomic told him that he had done it. What is being suggested here is that that was not true and that was a fabricated piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this is in the context, it seems to be accepted that the witness or the person Tomic is no longer alive?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What are the circumstances in which this statement was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The indicia of reliability are that it was compiled on the 14th of March before an investigating judge at the military court in Belgrade in relation to unknown perpetrators for the criminal offence. It was taken in front of an investigating judge, Trifunovic. There was a clerk. There was an interview as such, and that, if I may read: "Pursuant to Article 231, the witness was cautioned and he was obliged to tell the truth and he must not" -- actually, it says that "he must withhold any facts." But I'll read it. He was obliged to tell the truth and he must withhold any facts as giving false testimony was a criminal offence. I suspect the word "not" is missing there. Then it goes on to give the name of Tomic and the document itself is compiled. It is a -- basically a court-created document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The date is the 14th of March, 2000. And I'm very helpfully reminded by my learned friend, Ms. Regue that exactly the same process that was applied when Colonel Vujic was giving evidence and founded basis of credibility and arguments by my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I believe that in this way my learned friend is trying to introduce the substance of a statement that he has already tried to introduce pursuant to the 92 bis statement of Colonel Tomic. This was a proposal that the Trial Chamber overruled at the time. The witness is dead, and his statement speaks directly to the actions of the accused. We do not believe that this can be admitted based on Rule 92 bis. Aside from that, I believe that my learned friend is entirely wrong, as far as the basis for this is concerned. The Defence is not trying to contest the fact that Colonel Tomic may have told him that he had been to see Colonel Mrksic or whatever he told him if he did. All we did challenge was that Colonel Tomic was with Colonel Mrksic, but we did not challenge the fact that Colonel Vujic may have talked to Colonel Tomic about this and that Colonel Tomic may have told him this or that for one reason or another, mainly that he talked to Colonel Mrksic, which he didn't. This is not a circumstance affecting the credibility of a witness. We didn't say that Colonel Vujic was not speaking the truth when he talked about talking to Colonel Tomic. All we challenged was that Colonel Tomic ever went to see Colonel Mrksic. These are two very different things. In addition to this, we believe that introducing a statement, especially the relevant portion that my learned friend wishes to have read out, would run counter to a ruling of this Trial Chamber, the ruling of the Trial Chamber in relation to the OTP's request to use this statement under 92 bis. My learned friend, Mr. Lukic, has just reminded me that there was another legal issue just like this at stake in the Simic case, and the Chamber overruled a request like this that was made by the OTP in that case. If necessary, I believe that my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, can elaborate on that. Once again, the Defence is not challenging the fact that the late Colonel Tomic said something like this to Colonel Vujic, but what we are definitely challenging is that Colonel Tomic went to see Colonel Mrksic on that day. But what my learned friend said about Velepromet is not in Colonel Tomic's statement at all. Therefore, it can't be used in reference to this portion of the statement. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've been offered as a volunteer. Do you have a reference in Simic that's material?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In procedural terms, I believe that this is an identical situation. In the Simic case, the Prosecutor proposed at the very outset of the case to introduce into evidence an interview which OTP conducted with Miroslav Tadic, one of the accused. The Trial Chamber made a ruling - I'm not sure whether it was an oral or a written ruling - in September of 2002, refusing to admit into evidence these interviews, finding that they were not in a proper form -- or rather, that the form was deficient and didn't warrant them to be introduced into evidence. When the OTP -- rather, we had a Court's ruling that one of the documents could not be admitted into evidence; however, despite of that, the Prosecution still made a request to put certain parts of the interview to the witness. And once again the Trial Chamber overruled this saying that this could not be used to prove or disprove the credibility of a witness because, once again, the form of the interview was deficient. This Chamber in this case ruled that the statement of Mr. Tomic was deficient in its form, and thus could not be admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis. This is why I used this analogy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That decision was before Rule 89(F) came into existence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Firstly, I have a transcript of my learned friend Mr. Vasic's question. "You told us" -- may I just read it. "You told us what you heard Colonel Tomic saying to Colonel Mrksic about the fact that the TO wanted to take of the prisoners of war from the barracks by force. If I tell you that Colonel Mrksic -- was that Colonel Tomic in the presence of an air force colonel never said anything like that to him nor was Colonel Mrksic ever an advocate of the alleged idea that anyone should be treated with laxity, what would you say to that?" Now, there are two elements in that question: One, never said anything like that to him. I would submit it is as plain as a pike staff, if I may use an old English phrase, that that is what is being put, that it was not said by Tomic to Mrksic. Now, with regard to the distinction, and I believe there is an important distinction to be drawn here. One has to ask: What is the purpose of putting this statement in? If it's to be put in testimonially, namely for the truth of the content, that cannot be done. I accept that although it may well be there's a development on the law of that. But as matters stand, I accept that it cannot be put in for the truth of the content. And when in actual fact the application was made by the Prosecution under the 92 bis application, it was being put in for the truth of content. That was denied, perfectly rightly, by the Court. But what is the purpose now of this statement going in? It is not going in for the truth of the content. I would submit, it is going in, in relation to the consistency of the witness. It goes in to his credibility, and that is the important distinction, in my submission. With regard to this, what is being suggested by the Defence is that this witness an untrustworthy witness and a witness not to be believed, and they are putting to him an element that we submit should be before the Court for the Court to evaluate the overall credibility of the witness. And I rely on -- again, the Rules in relation to it. I rely on 89(F), as I have attempted to do before, that "it may receive the evidence of a witness orally or where the interests allow in written form." In my submission in the interests of justice in relation to the credibility of this witness, Vujic, it should be permitted. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clarify something to my learned friend. The Defence cannot be in the position to know whether Vujic and Tomic talked amongst themselves. We do not wish and are not even trying to deny that. All we're saying is this: If they talked then Tomic said something that was not true to Vujic. So we're not trying to challenge the credibility of Mr. Vujic through this; all we're doing is we're claiming there was no such conversation taking place with Mr. Tomic. Therefore, I think that my learned friend is not right about this fact. We do not have a single fact that could disprove whether Vujic and Tomic talked at all. As for Rule 89(F), I believe that here we are facing the same problem we discussed when my learned friend put his general submission for application of this rule. In this case, when we're discussing credibility, we could perhaps discuss the potential application of this Rule. However, this does not jeopardise the credibility of Mr. Vujic. His credibility is put at risk by means of some other submissions we made here. As for the acts of the accused, I think that our position is clear, namely that Rule 89(F) should not violate the principles set by 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, do we correctly understand that your question to the witness was, in essence: You told us you heard Tomic saying to Colonel Mrksic that the TO wanted to take prisoners of war from the barracks by force? Was that the thrust of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I asked, since Mr. Vujic said that Mr. Tomic told him about the meeting with Colonel Mrksic -- thus, I asked him what would be his position if I were to tell him that Mrksic never met Tomic, without challenging whether Tomic and Vujic ever talked. I don't know about that. I also don't know whether Colonel Tomic said the truth or not to Colonel Vujic about the meeting with Mr. Mrksic. So what we're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I put to you was what I understood to be the transcript that Mr. Moore read out. Did I misunderstand Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what Mr. Moore read out was that I put to the witness that Colonel Tomic and Colonel Mrksic did not talk about the relevant matter. That's one thing. Then I asked him this: You said that Colonel Tomic talked to you, telling you that he had been to see Colonel Mrksic. I'm telling you that he didn't see Colonel Mrksic. What is your comment? That was the substance of my question. Based on this question, it doesn't arise that I challenged whether Vujic talked to Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll just have Mr. Moore remind us of what it was that he read, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I've got here is day 52 of the transcript. I'm told the number is, I think, 4706.18. I, unfortunately, have not got an edited version, so may I just find that so I can read it out absolutely accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question is as follows. Thank you. "You told us what you heard Colonel Tomic saying to Colonel Mrksic about the fact that the TO wanted to take over the prisoners of war from the barracks by force. If I tell you that Colonel -- from Colonel Mrksic's standpoint was that Colonel Tomic, in the presence of an air force colonel, never said anything like that to him, nor was Colonel Mrksic ever an advocate of the alleged idea that anyone should be treated with laxity, what would you say to that?" Now, that is the -- my reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be then quite a dispute between what you understand you were putting, Mr. Vasic, and what the transcript suggests you were putting. I think, Mr. Vasic, in fairness we will let you contemplate this over the break so that you can be clear whether you accept that this was the question that you put to the witness or not. Will that be of use? And, if necessary, you and Mr. Moore can talk about the issue and we will return at five minutes past 6.00 and the witness should wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It seems to me that this break was beneficial, and I think I have discovered what the problem is. The problem is in the transcript, more or less. It seems that it does not reflect what I asked yesterday. As my learned friend read out, my question begins with: "You told us what you heard Colonel Tomic saying to Colonel Mrksic." I actually asked the witness: "You said what you heard from Colonel Tomic about him talking to Colonel Mrksic because Colonel Vujic was not present when that conversation took place," and that can be seen also on the basis of the answer the witness gave to my learned friend on page 4567, lines 11 to 14 of the transcript, when my learned friend said -- asked: "What about Tomic?" And the answer was: [In English] "Slavko Tomic said that he went because of that two or three times to see Colonel Mrksic to intervene in relation to these buses." [Interpretation] Based on the answer, we can see that Witness Vujic was not present when the conversation took place, and I couldn't challenge whether he heard the conversation between Tomic and Mrksic; quite the opposite. I asked Mr. Vujic: Based on the conversation with Mr. Tomic, what would his position be if I said that Tomic didn't see Mrksic. I don't know whether Tomic talked to Vujic and told him the truth or not. Thus, I did not challenge the credibility of Mr. Vujic. I think that the mistake lies in the interpretation as recorded in the transcript on the page that my learned friend mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, it does go to the credibility. It is -- it is put in very clear terms to the witness that -- in actual fact, that that never occurred. And so, therefore, I'm just trying to read exactly the way it was finally put. Would Your Honour forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just locating the original rather than what was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't got the transcript as it should be, but in any event the way that it was put was perfectly clear that it never said anything like that to him, nor was Colonel Mrksic ever an advocate. And so what is being suggested to Vujic was that Tomic had not spoken to Mrksic, and therefore the suggestion is that Vujic was, once again, fabricating the evidence. And all I'm submitting is if the credibility of this witness is to be considered, then the Court should have this particular piece of evidence from Tomic's statement - not all the statement - that relates quite clearly to Tomic going to Mrksic and stating what he says in the statement, warning about the prisoners of war and the barracks because it is evidence, if I may use the old-fashioned phrase, that corroborates what Vujic has been said. Now, corroboration deals with truth of content. I don't do it for that reason. I do it for the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic draws a distinction between there being a conversation between Tomic and Colonel Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's fair that we wait, Mr. Vasic, because Mr. Moore is being -- regrouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have it on one screen here to my right, bun unfortunately the microphone is to the left. Let me see if this microphone works. What I've got on the transcript is:" Thank you. You told us what you heard Colonel Tomic saying to Colonel Mrksic about the fact that the TO wanted to tell -- to take over the prisoners of war from the barracks by force. If I tell you that Colonel Mrksic's standpoint was that Colonel Tomic, in the presence of an air force colonel, never said anything like that to him, nor was Colonel Mrksic ever an advocate of the alleged idea that anyone should be treated with laxity, what would you say to that?" Now, that is, I hope, a verbatim reading of -- I think it will be 4706, line 18 to 25. My submission is that Colonel Vujic is having a question put to him that the account that he gave, namely, that Tomic had told Vujic that Tomic had been to Mrksic and expressed concerns about the TO and the behaviour at the barracks, what is being suggested there is that Vujic is fabricating his evidence. In my submission, because that question has been phrased the way it has, it brings into issue the credibility of Vujic's testimony. And again, in my submission, all I would wish to do is to adduce part of Tomic's statement which states that Tomic did, indeed, state in his witness statement that he did go to Mrksic and express those concerns on three occasions or on occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we start with the difficulty that Mr. Vasic now puts that this English translation is not the question that he put to the witness. And as he understands it, his question started not with, "You told us that you heard Colonel Tomic saying to Mrksic," but starts along the lines: You said what you heard from Colonel Tomic about him talking about Colonel Mrksic. And then Mr. Vasic draws a distinction between whether or not there was any conversation between Tomic and Colonel Mrksic as to which he says we have no dispute, we accept there was, but that what we did dispute was the content of that conversation. And it's not that the witness said: I actually heard the conversation, but that the witness merely has -- recounts what Tomic told him later about that conversation. And on that footing he says: We are disputing the accuracy of what this witness heard from Tomic about the conversation between Tomic and Mrksic, but we are not disputing that the witness may have been told that by Tomic. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I agree -- I accept my learned friend if he says that the translation is in error. I will accept, of course, the word of my learned friend on that. And therefore, I imagine that the transcript will have to be looked at again, irrespective of whether it is a finished product. In my submission, it matters not. The issue is that Mr. Vasic, upon instructions, is clearly saying to this witness, Vujic: You are fabricating your evidence in certain respects with regard to, as I say, the other matter at Negoslavci, but here in relation to the barracks, because what this witness is saying is that Tomic told him he had been to see Mrksic. Now, what is being said here by my learned friend Mr. Vasic is: Well, that never happened. No such conversation with Tomic or Mrksic ever occurred. And irrespective of whether you get it right or wrong, that conversation never occurred. Mrksic never was told that. And therefore, in my submission, the issue is: Is Vujic to be believed on what Tomic said to him? Because what Tomic said to him is admissible as evidence against Mrksic. It may well be in our definition hearsay, but the fact of the matter it is admissible as evidence against Mrksic. Consequently, if my submission, if there is an attack on the credibility of this witness and it is said: Was that conversation between Tomic and Mrksic never occurred, in my submission the Court is entitled to look at the totality of the evidence in relation to this topic, not for the truth of the content of what Tomic says, but the fact that Tomic himself did indicate in his statement that he had been to Mrksic. It goes to the credibility of the witness, not to the truth of the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The proposition you put is clearly materially affected by what the question actually was, and that, I think, is something that the Chamber may have to have determined by a reconsideration of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we'll get it accurately and fully set out so we know what it was. But if you go on further, if you look at the question, as we understand the second part of it is, at least from the English - and again, this may be subject to further consideration from the tape - that my client's standpoint is that in the presence of an air force colonel, Tomic never said anything like that, does seem to carry the implication that there was a conversation, it was in the presence of an air force colonel, but its content was different from what this witness understood from Tomic to be the content. The question is whether it is this witness's credibility or Tomic's credibility that's being called in question, if that is a correct rendition of what the question was about. Mr. Moore, let's see if we can deal with this constructively, given the hour. If everything you put was right and was accepted, what is it that you would have this witness say? What sort of question would you contemplate putting to him? One question, whether the relevant part of the transcript of the deceased Tomic should be received in evidence on the question of credibility; another issue, and this is what I'm putting to you now, is what can this witness contribute to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour has hit the nail on the head. I, for my part, would see no reason for the witness to be delayed or to be re-called. We can look at the accuracy of the transcript. The legal argument will be determined one way or other. And for my part - I don't know what the Defence position would be - I would then seek for that extraction, this part of the statement, to be put in as evidence. It's not -- I was going to put it through the witness, but it's perfectly possible for this to go in as evidence, which is self-supporting. So for my part, it could go in that way without having to re-call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Moore, we are approaching a solution to the present situation. The Chamber sees the precise form of the questioning and the answer to be material. There -- we understand from Mr. Vasic's rendition in English, which may not be accurate. We will need to have the actual form of question and answer confirmed. That will take time, and we therefore propose to delay reaching a decision on the admissibility of this extract from the document until we can be assured about the actual question and answer that you found your present application on. And we do that in the understanding at the moment that even if your position is proved to be sound, we don't see that this witness can contribute anything more to the matter one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has said: "I heard certain things from Tomic," and that will, if we ever come to receive the written document, be borne out or not borne out by whatever the deceased Tomic has said. So we can, for the moment, defer a decision on your motion. We heard what Mr. Vasic has to say, and we accept that there's need and reason to have the exact translation confirmed, and we will have that done and deal with the matter in due course when we get a confirmed form of the question and answer. Could I just indicate that this is, in our view, not a matter that arises under 92 bis and is not determined by the decision that was given on the 92 bis application because the decision on 92 bis was on a motion under a very precise rule which allows the admissibility for the truth of its content of written statements which do not touch the actual acts and conduct of an accused person. What is now being proposed is something quite different, that is on a question of credibility whether we should receive this statement in confirmation or otherwise of the evidence given by this witness. So we mention that so that you understand that we see Rule 92 bis as not determinative of the issue one way or the other. And if it is received, this document, I think, if we needed a rule, would be received under Rule 89, perhaps under (B) or (C), but we will worry about that if the case arises. So we will defer that matter until we get the correct interpretation. You've got something further, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, something that may be of assistance to the Chamber and to everybody else. I don't think there's any dispute, even from my learned friend, about the fact that Mr. Vujic was not present when Mr. Tomic and when Mr. Mrksic allegedly talked. Therefore, I could not possibly have asked him whether he had heard this conversation. It was just one thing that I wanted to clarify. I think that is beyond dispute, and in this context I think the nature of my original question is quite clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, that concludes the evidence of the witness. He should be informed that he may leave. Mr. Moore, are you ready with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I have a witness who is here and ready to give evidence, if I may reply in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you're getting as cagey as Mr. Vasic over that last question. Can I say that I have a need to finish at a quarter to 7.00 tonight. Is it practical, do you think, to commence the new witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I, for my part, think it's better for a witness to settle and then just proceed to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any concern about an early break this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope my learned friend will be happy to see us cooperate on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I am grateful to counsel; it assists me. We will then adjourn early and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.32 p.m.,
